extracted.intended_audience: criminal judges, investigators, and forensic experts
extracted.subtask_description: Practical standards for judges and criminal investigators on handling secrets, confessions, witnesses, experts, and the observation of external (phenomenological) signs. Emphasises tact, independent corroboration, sustaining interest, and cautious use of behavioural cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding official secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Official secrets have a general significance, and must therefore be guarded at all points and not merely in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'blabbing' even seemingly harmless bare facts; half-truths can cause vexatious errors by association and circumscriptive limitations. Be mindful that repeated or widely communicated bare facts will combine with other information and may disclose sensitive matters. Do not assume omission of names/places/time makes disclosure safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's silence about known matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Never reveal what is already known; silence must be considered in both directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding known facts is a trade-off — premature or garrulous disclosure can suggest conclusions, mislead witnesses, or create false impressions; but excessive secrecy may deprive the examiner of examination tools. Rule: never move toward incorrectness and never present the appearance of knowing more than you actually do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of optima fide errors (believing possibilities as facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware the danger of knowing something untrue—especially for those skilled at synthesis and inference (optima fide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talented, courageous examiners are most at risk of converting possibilities into perceived certainties. Whether a falsehood arises from deliberate lie or over-sanguine temperament, the practitioner must exercise caution and check inferences against evidence rather than assume them true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing disclosure of third-party secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: When an actual secret is recognized, consider whether damage is greater through keeping it or revealing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally prefer not to force secrets from witnesses (torturing secrets causes damage). If convinced that revelation is necessary (e.g., to protect an innocent), apply all skill and effort; ensure no hint of bad faith when revealing, and proceed cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid eagerness when eliciting secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief rule is not to be overeager in getting at the desired secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lead directly for the secret; many important facts will surface spontaneously. Eagerness can turn trivial facts into guarded secrets. If every other means fails, cautiously reveal a little more of the crime to the witness (carefully focusing on episodes that cluster around the secret) so the witness sees the importance of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand types and motives of confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Confessions arise from diverse motives (mitigation, vanity, convenience, conscience, nobility, deception, political reasons, death-bed, religious confession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise varied psychological and social reasons for confession (including false or misleading confessions). Do not treat confession as self-explanatory; classify and evaluate motive to inform further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession as means of proof, not conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of caution all statutes approve confessions as evidence only when they agree completely with the other evidence. Confession is a means of proof, and not proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require objective, evidentially concurrent support and confirmation for confessions. The corroborative evidence must have been arrived at independently; otherwise the suggestive power of the confession may distort all other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fit evidence to confession — evaluate independently
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge must not fit all testimony to the already furnished confession, allowing the evidence to serve as mere decoration to the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pigeon-holing: establish proof by means of the confession AND by other evidence independently. If a judge adapts other evidence to match a confession, false confessions will not be discovered and the search for truth is abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling witnesses when a confession exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When a confession exists, the witness should be told of it and that it is not yet evidence, and the judge must prevent the witness from presenting evidence in light of the confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain to witnesses (when permissible) that a confession exists but emphasise its provisional status. Keep a calm, controlled approach so witnesses do not color testimony to fit the confession. Where possible, ask intelligent witnesses to give testimony 'as if there were no confession' and analyze their answers elementally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elemental analysis of testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze testimony into its elements to determine what, taken in itself, is a material element and what merely appears to be one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each reported incident, ask: without the confession, would this fact incriminate? Consider alternative interpretations, timing, causation, and whether different observers might construe events differently (example: sequence during a brawl and whether someone had time to stab).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for dealing with less intelligent witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnesses cannot perform constructive analysis, use general rules: demand complete accuracy and insist on the ratio sciendi (how they came to know it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on precise reporting and on the witness explaining the reasons and means of their knowledge. Such insistence often converts uncertain perceptions into trustworthy statements regarding the confessor; when untrue confessions are suspected, careful critical comparison of testimony can reveal adaptation due to suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of suggestive influence of prior evidence or arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: People are readily influenced by antecedent grounds of suspicion (e.g., seeing a suspect in prison garb or knowing an arrest was made).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow witnesses to take the fact of arrest or pre-existing suspicion as corroboration; continue investigation only with caution and attempt to elicit unprejudiced identification. Keep the examination focused on what is known, avoiding psychological ὑστερον προτερον (seeing corroboration because action was taken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arousing and sustaining interest of collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Anybody who means to work honestly must strive to awaken and to sustain the interest of his collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present material well-arranged, systematic, exhaustive but not redundant; be minutely informed on the case. Interest yields attention and better effort from colleagues and experts. Avoid indifference: show that you value the expert's task and input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperating effectively with experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts must be convinced of the judge's complete interest in their work and of the judge's power to value the effort and knowledge required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have some insight into the relevant disciplines enough to converse intelligibly; read expert reports attentively; ask for elucidation where unclear. Demonstrated interest motivates better, more careful expert work and benefits the state and case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for arousing witness interest and attention
rubrics_metrics.description: No interest, no attention — the absolutely new does not stimulate; attention must be generated, not commanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how a question or fact relates to the case and why it matters for investigation. Use circumstantial explanations and associated memories to help witnesses recall. Balance the amount of information given: do not tell delicate matters to unknown witnesses prematurely; consider recalling a witness later when fuller information can be given safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenology: cautious inference from outward signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomenology is the systematic coordination of outer symptoms occasioned by inner processes; but unquestionable inferences from appearance to mental state are not yet possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat outward expressions as semiotic indicators subject to error: observations are insufficiently numerous and accurate, individual variation is large, and physiological/habitual factors confound direct inference. Use phenomenology to critique popular inferences and reduce exaggerated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General external conditions of mental states
rubrics_metrics.description: Every state of consciousness has its physical correlate, but identical inner states do not invariably have identical bodily concomitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with generalization: bodily concomitants may be indirect, accidental habits or inheritances may mould expression, phenomena are often personal and variable, and purely physiological conditions (blushing, trembling, laughter) affect expression. Treat gestures as possible truthful contradictions of words but verify carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observing and interpreting gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures are powerful habitual expressions and often contradict words; but there are dangers in overvaluing or publicising gesture-observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin studies with the most dangerous cases (murder/robbery); start with simple daily-life cases to develop practice. Avoid wrongly attributing meaning to habitual gestures, avoid making observations so noticeable that witnesses control them, and balance the difficulty of watching gestures with other investigative duties. Properly practised, gesture observation is valuable and often rewarding.
